content: Severe malaria is responsible for over a million deaths annually, with the majority of these fatalities occurring in children under the age of five who reside in sub-Saharan Africa. This study aimed to determine whether artesunate, as an alternative to the standard treatment quinine, could lead to improved survival rates and better treatment outcomes for patients with severe malaria. To address this question, researchers conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. They searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, ISI Web of Science, and others, up until November 2010. The review included studies that compared intravenous, intramuscular, or rectal artesunate with intravenous or intramuscular quinine in adults and children with severe malaria who were unable to take oral medications. The primary outcome of interest was all-cause mortality. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of the trials, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data for analysis. Dichotomous outcomes were summarized using risk ratios (RR), while continuous outcomes were analyzed using mean differences (MD). When appropriate, data were pooled in meta-analyses. The review included eight trials involving a total of 1664 adults and 5765 children. The findings demonstrated that treatment with artesunate significantly reduced the risk of death in both adults and children. In adults, the risk of death was reduced by 39% (RR 0.61, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.50 to 0.75; 1664 participants, five trials). In children, the risk of death was reduced by 24% (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.90; 5765 participants, four trials). However, in children, the use of artesunate was associated with an increased incidence of neurological sequelae at the time of hospital discharge. Most of these neurological complications were transient, and no significant differences in neurological outcomes were observed between artesunate and quinine at later follow-up assessments. In conclusion, the evidence strongly supports the use of parenteral artesunate over quinine for the treatment of severe malaria in both adults and children across different regions of the world. Artesunate is associated with a significant reduction in mortality, making it the superior treatment option for severe malaria.
